roman_terminus.name: Cannot be moved or yield even to Jupiter, fixing every boundary forever
roman_terminus.notes: When the Capitol was cleared for the temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, every god's shrine yielded to augury except Terminus, who refused to move; his immovability was read as an omen of Rome's eternal, unshrinkable borders.

sources.reference: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 1.55; Ovid, Fasti 2.667-678
Dumezil, Archaic Roman Religion

roman_venilia.name: Embodies the breaking surface-waves that run to shore
roman_venilia.notes: Varro derived her name from the wave that 'comes' (venit) to land; as paredra of Neptune she personifies the onrushing surf, paired against Salacia of the open deep.

sources.reference: Augustine, De Civitate Dei 7.22; Varro in Aulus Gellius, Noctes Atticae 13.23

roman_vertumnus.name: Turns the year and ripens the orchard's fruit through the seasons
roman_vertumnus.notes: As god of vertere, the 'turning' of the seasons, he brings garden and orchard produce to ripeness; the first-fruits and the turning year are his province.

sources.reference: Propertius, Elegies 4.2; Ovid, Metamorphoses 14.623-697

roman_vesta.name: Is present as the living flame itself rather than in any image
roman_vesta.notes: Vesta was worshipped not as a statue but as the fire of her aedes; her temple held no cult-image, the goddess being identified with the undying flame whose extinction portended disaster for Rome.

sources.reference: Ovid, Fasti 6.291-298; Cicero, De Natura Deorum 2.27

sabaean_shams.name: Shines as patron sun-goddess and tutelary of the royal house
sabaean_shams.notes: Worshippers turned east and prayed at sunrise, noon and sunset; she protected the Sabaean and later Himyarite dynasty as their burning solar patroness.

sources.reference: Sabaean dedicatory inscriptions (RES, CIH corpora)
Robin, 'Le pantheon des Arabes du Sud'

sabaean_sin.name: Reigns as national god and oracular lord of Hadramawt
sabaean_sin.notes: Sayin (Syn) was the supreme deity of the Hadrami kingdom, his chief temple at the capital Shabwa; the kingdom's caravan incense trade was placed under his protection.

sources.reference: Hadrami inscriptions; coinage of Hadramawt (Shabwa mint)
Beeston, in Studies in the History of Arabia

sabaean_wadd.name: Wards and protects his people, who invoke 'Wadd is father'
sabaean_wadd.notes: The Minaeans inscribed the formula Wd 'b ('Wadd is father') on amulets, doorways and temple walls as an apotropaic protection for person and town.

sources.reference: Minaean inscriptions of the Jawf (e.g. inscription M 244, Qarnawu/Yathill)
Robin, 'Le pantheon des Arabes du Sud'

salish_old_one.name: Names and assigns to each being its nature and place in the world
salish_old_one.notes: In the Interior Salish cosmogony the Old One / Chief, dwelling alone above, brings the world and its first beings into order and apportions to each its role before sending the transformers to finish the work.

sources.reference: Teit, Mythology of the Thompson Indians (Jesup North Pacific Expedition)

sami_beaivi.name: Restores the greening of the land and the fertility of the reindeer herds
sami_beaivi.notes: As she climbs higher after the polar night Beaivi quickens the growth of plants and the increase of the herds; she is invoked as the giver of new life to land and animals.

sources.reference: Holmberg (Harva), Lapland sacrifices; Karsten, The Religion of the Samek

sami_horagalles.name: Bends the rainbow as his bow to shoot down trolls and evil spirits
sami_horagalles.notes: The rainbow is 'Aijeke's bow' (Aijeke dauge); with it, with his hammers, and with lightning, Horagalles hunts and destroys the harmful spirits and trolls that haunt the rocks and fells.

sources.reference: Leem, Beskrivelse over Finmarkens Lapper; Friis, Lappisk Mythologi

sami_horagalles.name: Governs sky, weather, lakes and seas, and human health and welfare
sami_horagalles.notes: Beyond thunder and lightning Horagalles is lord of the weather, the rainbow, the waters, and the life and health of people and livestock.

sources.reference: Friis, Lappisk Mythologi

sami_jabmeahkka.name: Clothes the dead in a new body and shelters the souls of dead children
sami_jabmeahkka.notes: In Jabmiaimo the dead receive a new body in place of the one decaying above, and are as powerful there as they were in life; the souls of infants are held to be especially comforted by her.

sources.reference: Holmberg (Harva), Lapland sacrifices; Karsten, The Religion of the Samek

sami_leib_olmai.name: Appears to hunters in the shape of a bear and grants or withholds the hunt
sami_leib_olmai.notes: Lord of the forest game and especially of the bear, Leib-olmai shows himself as a bear; hunters depended on his favour for success and made him offerings before and after the chase.

sources.reference: Holmberg (Harva), Finno-Ugric and Siberian Mythology; Karsten, The Religion of the Samek

sami_mano.name: Rules the dark season, when noise is forbidden and evil spirits walk
sami_mano.notes: The masculine moon was worshipped about the new moon and at midwinter; his was a perilous season of wandering spirits, observed with a taboo on making any noise.

sources.reference: Holmberg (Harva), Lapland sacrifices; Karsten, The Religion of the Samek

sami_madder_attje.name: Stands as the ancestral father, male counterpart of the origin-mother
sami_madder_attje.notes: Madder-attje ('root/ancestor-father') is the consort of Maderakka; in some accounts he receives the soul from the high god and passes it to Maderakka, who forms its body, though his role is far smaller than hers and held to be a later addition.

sources.reference: Holmberg (Harva), Lapland sacrifices; Friis, Lappisk Mythologi

sami_radien_akka.name: Receives the soul from the high god to be passed down for new birth
sami_radien_akka.notes: As the celestial mother of the Radien family she shares in the transmission of the soul: the high god sends it, and through the family it descends by way of Maderakka to be born.

sources.reference: Holmberg (Harva), Lapland sacrifices; Friis, Lappisk Mythologi

sami_rana_niejta.name: Greens the spring hillsides so the slopes bear new growth for the reindeer
sami_rana_niejta.notes: Her name ('Rana, the green hillside' + niejta, 'maiden') marks her as the power of the greening land; she was petitioned in spring that the fells should put forth new pasture for the herds.

sources.reference: Friis, Lappisk Mythologi; Holmberg (Harva), Lapland sacrifices

roman_saturnus.name: the Saturnalia
roman_saturnus.notes: Rome's most exuberant festival: a public sacrifice at the temple of Saturn ritu Graeco (with head uncovered) and a lectisternium, followed by feasting, gift-giving (sigillaria), the freeing of the statue's woolen bonds, license, gambling, and the reversal of master and slave.

sources.reference: Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.7-10; Livy 22.1.19-20

roman_sol.name: festival of Sol Invictus (dies natalis Solis Invicti)
roman_sol.cadence: 25 December (with games of Sol every fourth year)
roman_sol.notes: Aurelian established a state cult of Sol Invictus in 274 CE with a college of pontifices Solis and a great temple in the Campus Agrippae; games (agon Solis) and the birthday of the Unconquered Sun on 25 December honoured the god as supreme protector of the empire.

sources.reference: Historia Augusta, Aurelian; Chronograph of 354

roman_terminus.name: the Terminalia
roman_terminus.notes: Neighbouring landowners met at their shared boundary-stone, garlanded it, raised an altar, and offered grain, honeycombs and wine, the stone drenched with the blood of a sacrificed lamb or suckling pig; a communal feast affirmed the inviolability of the border.

sources.reference: Ovid, Fasti 2.639-684

roman_tiberinus.name: the ludi piscatorii (fishermen's games) and Tiberinalia
roman_tiberinus.cadence: ludi piscatorii on 7 June; offerings at the Insula Tiberina
roman_tiberinus.notes: The Tiber's fishermen held games in his honour on 7 June; offerings were cast into the river and made at his shrine on the Insula Tiberina to keep the waters calm and the floods at bay.

sources.reference: Ovid, Fasti; Roman calendar; Festus on the ludi piscatorii

roman_vesta.name: the Vestalia
roman_vesta.notes: During the Vestalia the penus Vestae was opened to Roman matrons who entered barefoot to make offerings; the Vestal Virgins prepared the mola salsa, the temple was swept and purified, and mill-donkeys were garlanded and rested. The undying fire was renewed each 1 March.

sources.reference: Ovid, Fasti 6.249-468

roman_vertumnus.name: the Vortumnalia
roman_vertumnus.notes: Offerings of the season's first fruits and flowers were made to Vertumnus (shared with Pomona); his bronze statue at the signum Vortumni in the Vicus Tuscus was decked according to the changing season.

sources.reference: Varro, De Lingua Latina 5.46; Propertius, Elegies 4.2

roman_volcanus.name: the Volcanalia
roman_volcanus.notes: At the height of summer fire-danger live fish from the Tiber (and small animals) were thrown into the bonfire at the Vulcanal as substitute-life, dying in place of men so that destructive fire would spare the granaries and farms.

sources.reference: Varro, De Lingua Latina 6.20; Pliny, Naturalis Historia

sabaean_almaqah.name: pilgrimage and oracle at the Awwam temple of Marib
sabaean_almaqah.notes: The vast oval temple of Awwam (the 'Mahram Bilqis') near Marib was Almaqah's chief sanctuary and oracular seat from at least the 7th century BCE, drawing pilgrims of the Sabaean confederation who left thousands of votive dedications.

sources.reference: Sabaean inscriptions of the Awwam temple (RES, CIH)
Robin, 'Le pantheon des Arabes du Sud'

sami_beaivi.name: midwinter white-animal sacrifice to the returning sun
sami_beaivi.notes: A white female reindeer (or other white animal) was sacrificed at midwinter to bring the sun back and renew fertility; the meat was threaded on sticks bent into rings and tied with bright ribbons, sacrificial porridge was set out, and butter was smeared on the doorposts so the sun could regain strength and climb higher.

sources.reference: Holmberg (Harva), Lapland sacrifices; Karsten, The Religion of the Samek

sami_leib_olmai.name: the bear-feast and the alder-bark rite
sami_leib_olmai.cadence: at the killing of a bear; daily offerings by hunters
sami_leib_olmai.notes: After a bear was killed the hunters chewed alder bark to a red, blood-like juice and sprinkled it on themselves, the bear, the dogs and the draught-reindeer, singing songs of thanks to the bear and to Leib-olmai; small bows and arrows were offered to him for luck in the hunt.

sources.reference: Holmberg (Harva), Finno-Ugric and Siberian Mythology

sami_horagalles.name: offering of reindeer antlers and metal at the thunder-god's site
sami_horagalles.notes: A local cult on the island of Aijih-sualui (Ukonsaari) in Lake Inari received offerings of reindeer antlers and metal objects to the thunder-god; idols of him bore an iron nail in the head as his fire.

sources.reference: Friis, Lappisk Mythologi; archaeological finds, Ukonsaari, Inari

sami_radien_attje.name: sacrifice of a male reindeer at the world-pillar
sami_radien_attje.cadence: occasional, to keep the world from collapsing
sami_radien_attje.notes: A forked tree on the sacrificial altar represented the world-pillar (veralden tsuold) by which Radien-attje upholds the cosmos; a male reindeer or other animal was sacrificed so that he would not let the world fall.

sources.reference: Holmberg (Harva), Lapland sacrifices; Friis, Lappisk Mythologi

samoan_nafanua.name: oracular consultation before war at Falealupo
samoan_nafanua.notes: Chiefs from distant villages and islands came to her sanctuary at Falealupo on Savaii (also the entrance to Pulotu) to seek her blessing and war-prophecy before a campaign; her famous oracle to Malietoa promised a crown from heaven.

sources.reference: Kramer, Die Samoa-Inseln; Turner, Samoa, a Hundred Years Ago and Long Before

samoan_lefee.name: war-oracle at the Fale o le Fee
samoan_lefee.notes: Le Fee the octopus war-god was consulted for omens of war, his voice heard as thunder, at the Fale o le Fee, the only stone temple in Samoa, in the districts of Aana and Vaimauga.

sources.reference: Turner, Samoa, a Hundred Years Ago and Long Before; Stair, Old Samoa

attributes.name: veiled head and aged, bearded form
attributes.notes: Saturn was depicted as an old, bearded man with his head covered by a white veil; sacrifice to him was uniquely made with the head uncovered (ritu Graeco).

sources.reference: Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.8; Pompeian fresco of veiled Saturn

attributes.name: the curved pruning-sickle (falx / harpe)
attributes.notes: His defining emblem is the agricultural sickle, later read also as the scythe of Time.

sources.reference: Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.7-8; Roman statuary and gems

attributes.name: radiate crown (corona radiata) of sun-rays
attributes.notes: Sol is shown as a youthful figure crowned with a spiked nimbus of solar rays, often with the right hand raised.

sources.reference: Imperial coinage of Sol Invictus (Aurelian and later)

attributes.name: the four-horse chariot (quadriga) driven across the sky
attributes.notes: He drives the radiant chariot of the day, frequently holding a globe or whip, sometimes standing on a globe.

sources.reference: Roman coinage and reliefs of Sol in his quadriga

attributes.name: the boundary-stone (terminus / cippus), sometimes a herm
attributes.notes: He is the immovable border-stone itself, occasionally rendered as a bust rising from a column or as an uncarved planted stone anointed and garlanded at the Terminalia.

sources.reference: Ovid, Fasti 2.639-684; Siculus Flaccus, De Condicionibus Agrorum

attributes.name: bearded river-god reclining, crowned with reeds, holding cornucopia and oar
attributes.notes: The conventional river-god type: a bearded man reclining on the riverbank, reed-crowned, with cornucopia and steering-oar, often with the wolf and the twins Romulus and Remus.

sources.reference: Tiber colossus, Piazza del Campidoglio; Virgil, Aeneid 8.31-34
Virgil, Aeneid 8.34

attributes.name: the sacred flame (imageless cult)
attributes.notes: Vesta has no statue in her round temple; she is present as the eternal fire, the goddess being one with the flame the Vestals tend.

sources.reference: Ovid, Fasti 6.295-298; Cicero, De Natura Deorum 2.27

sacredAnimals.name: the donkey (whose bray woke her from Priapus; garlanded at the Vestalia)

sources.reference: Ovid, Fasti 6.319-348

attributes.name: ever-changing form, decked with garden produce
attributes.notes: Having no fixed shape, Vertumnus is shown wreathed with the fruits, grain and flowers of the changing seasons; in the Pomona tale he takes the guise of reaper, vine-dresser, soldier and old woman.

sources.reference: Ovid, Metamorphoses 14.643-656; Propertius, Elegies 4.2

attributes.name: the conical workman's cap (pileus) and hammer
attributes.notes: Vulcan is shown as a bearded craftsman in the brimless felt cap of labourers, bent at his anvil with hammer and tongs.

sources.reference: Roman reliefs and gems of Vulcan at the forge

attributes.name: a cluster of lightning-bolts about a curved sickle-like weapon

sources.reference: Robin, 'Le pantheon des Arabes du Sud'; Hofner in Worterbuch der Mythologie
